content.text: Lighthouse loads your page once, on one simulated phone, with nobody using it.
Core Web Vitals

are judged on real visits: LCP, INP and CLS at the 75th percentile, from Chrome users over 28 days. A perfect score can sit next to a failing assessment, because a single lab load can't see interactions, late layout shifts or your users' devices.

A product page with a filter button and a promo that appears once the visitor scrolls. We ran Lighthouse 13.6.0 from its command line with the default mobile settings against headless Chromium 156: Performance 100, CLS 0, Total Blocking Time 0 ms. Then a Playwright script loaded the same page in the same browser, scrolled once and tapped the filter. CLS reached 0.20, and that one tap took 304 ms from input to the next frame. Both values are in the "needs improvement" band. They're still lab numbers from a scripted visit, not field data, but they're exactly the kind of thing field data records and a page load never triggers.
The common misconception
The belief: a perfect Lighthouse score means the site passes Core Web Vitals for real users.

It's an understandable mix-up. Lighthouse reports LCP and CLS by name, uses the same green, orange and red bands, and PageSpeed Insights shows its score right below the field assessment. The score is also the one number you control: it runs in CI, it changes the minute you deploy, and it rewards real fixes. For a cold first load on a mid-range phone, it is a fair approximation. Core Web Vitals just aren't measured on that load.
What actually happens
Core Web Vitals are a verdict on real visits

web.dev defines three metrics and a "good" target for each, judged at the 75th percentile of page loads, segmented across mobile and desktop. A page passes when all three are good at that percentile. PageSpeed Insights takes these numbers from the
Chrome UX Report
(CrUX), covering the previous 28 days, and its assessment uses only LCP and CLS when there isn't enough INP data.

The slowest interaction, from input to the next frame, ignoring outliers
The largest burst of unexpected layout shifts

content.text: Anything between the two columns needs improvement. Why the 75th percentile? The thresholds article explains it's high enough that most visits meet the target, without letting a few outliers decide. The same thresholds apply to mobile and desktop, and most were set by what mobile can achieve.
The Lighthouse score is a different formula

The Performance score is a weighted average of five lab metrics. In Lighthouse 13.6.0, the version we ran: Total Blocking Time 30%, LCP 25%, CLS 25%, First Contentful Paint 10% and Speed Index 10%. Two of the five aren't Core Web Vitals, and INP isn't there at all. The scoring docs even call a 100 "extremely challenging to achieve and not expected", and say much of the run-to-run variability doesn't come from Lighthouse itself.
What a single load can't see
Interactions.

web.dev is explicit: tools that load a page in a simulated environment without a user can't measure INP, because there is no input. Total Blocking Time, built from long tasks during load, is the lab proxy, and web.dev warns that a page can have poor INP despite a very good TBT. Our filter button did nothing during load, so TBT stayed at 0.
Shifts after load.
CLS in the lab only counts shifts above the fold during load. In the field, it covers unexpected shifts during the whole life of the page, including the promo that appears after a scroll.
Your users' conditions.

The lab is one device on one network, usually with a cold cache. PageSpeed Insights simulates a mid-tier phone on a mobile network. Real visitors bring older phones, warm caches, other viewports and even a different LCP element.
Which numbers to trust for what

web.dev's advice is simple: when you have both, field data decides what to prioritize, and the lab is for debugging and for testing changes before they ship. A lab run is reproducible, which makes it great for catching regressions in CI. It just answers a different question from the field.
Measure your own users

CrUX only covers public, indexable URLs with enough samples from opted-in Chrome users, so a new page, a quiet one or anything behind a login may have no field data at all. web.dev recommends collecting your own field data anyway, because it's more actionable than CrUX alone. The web-vitals library measures the three metrics with standard browser APIs, the way Chrome does, and reports CLS and INP when the page is hidden. A hand-rolled snapshot at load misses most of it:

content.text: In PageSpeed Insights, the Core Web Vitals assessment at the top comes from CrUX; the score below it comes from a single Lighthouse run. When they disagree, the top section describes your users and the bottom section helps you find why.

The CrUX numbers in PageSpeed Insights cover the previous 28 days, so a fix you ship today is averaged with weeks of older visits for a while. Check your own monitoring for the trend, and don't roll back a good change because the assessment hasn't moved yet.
How to apply it in your project
Run your key URLs through PageSpeed Insights, or open Search Console's Core Web Vitals report, and note which metric fails, on which device type, at the 75th percentile.
Add the web-vitals library, send each metric with the page and device type, and chart the 75th percentile per metric. That covers pages CrUX doesn't, and shows a fix within days.
Use the failing metric to pick the lab tool: Lighthouse or the Performance panel for LCP, a recorded interaction for INP, a scroll through the page with layout shift regions on for CLS.
Run it in CI with a budget per metric rather than a demand for 100, and treat a drop as a hint to investigate.
Key takeaways

items.text: Core Web Vitals pass when LCP, INP and CLS are all good at the 75th percentile of real visits.
Good means LCP of 2.5 s or less, INP of 200 ms or less and CLS of 0.1 or less.
The Lighthouse score weighs five lab metrics, includes TBT and Speed Index, and can't measure INP.
A lab load misses interactions, shifts after load and your users' devices, caches and viewports.
Prioritize with field data, debug with lab data, and measure your own users with the web-vitals library.
